title: Detergent & Cleaning Products Production: A Six-Product Workshop
subtitle: Run safe, recorded production batches of six household and institutional cleaning products, test and pack them properly, and price them for profit.
description: A hands-on production course. You will neutralise sulphonic acid into liquid laundry detergent, fill dish liquid by weight, find the right dose for a floor cleaner, and make a citric acid toilet gel, an ammonia-free glass cleaner and a BKC disinfectant cleaner, then release each batch against a test card, pack it in the right container and cost it to the bottle.

Convert percentage formulas into kilograms and neutralise LABSA with caustic soda to a target pH
Produce liquid laundry detergent, dishwashing liquid, floor cleaner, toilet gel, glass and multi-surface sprays and a BKC disinfectant cleaner

modules.title: Cleaning Science and a Safe Production Room
modules.overview: Before you mix anything, you need to know why each product works, what every raw material in your store is, and how to set up a room where acids, alkalis and bleach can never meet by accident. This module builds that foundation for the six products you will make in Modules 2 and 3.

lessons.title: Matching the product to the dirt: surfactants, pH and the four cleaning forces
objectives: Explain in plain words how a surfactant lifts grease off a surface
Use the pH scale to choose an acid, neutral or alkaline cleaner for a given type of dirt
Describe the four cleaning forces and how changing one changes the others
Recommend the right product from the six in this course for a customer's cleaning problem

blocks.text: Every product in this course does one or more of three jobs: it **lifts dirt** (grease, oil, food, body soil), it **dissolves deposits** (limescale, rust stains, urine scale), or it **kills germs** on a surface. A production business that understands these three jobs makes fewer mistakes, sells the right product to each customer and writes honest directions on the label.

blocks.name: bubbles
blocks.caption: Foam is a sign that surfactant is present, but cleaning power comes from what happens at the surface of the dirt.

blocks.text: Surfactants: the molecules that do the lifting

Water alone cannot remove grease because oil and water do not mix. A **surfactant** (short for surface active agent) is a molecule with two ends. One end loves water. The other end loves oil. When you wash, the oil-loving ends push into the grease and the water-loving ends stay in the water. With rubbing, the grease breaks into tiny droplets that are surrounded by surfactant, so they float away in the rinse water instead of settling back.
Surfactants are grouped by the electric charge on the water-loving end. You will use three groups in this course:

items: **Anionic** (negative charge): LAS, made from sulphonic acid, and SLES (sold as "texapon"). Strong cleaners and good foamers. The base of laundry and dish products.
**Nonionic** (no charge): alcohol ethoxylates such as the AEO-9 grade. Good on oily soil, low foam, and they still work in acid products and next to disinfectants.
**Cationic** (positive charge): benzalkonium chloride (BKC), a quaternary ammonium compound used as a disinfectant. Weak cleaner, but it kills many germs.

blocks.title: Opposite charges cancel each other
blocks.text: Anionic and cationic surfactants attract each other and form a sticky, cloudy complex that does neither job well. Never add BKC to a dish liquid or laundry detergent made with LAS or SLES. You will see this with your own eyes in Lesson 3.3.
pH: choosing acid or alkaline

The **pH scale** runs from 0 to 14. Pure water is 7 (neutral). Below 7 is acid; above 7 is alkaline. Each step is ten times stronger than the one next to it, so pH 2 is ten times more acidic than pH 3. You will measure pH with paper strips (cheap, good enough to start) or a pen-type pH meter (more exact, needs calibration).

blocks.text: The four cleaning forces

Cleaning experts describe four forces that work together, often drawn as a circle: **chemistry** (the product), **action** (scrubbing, agitation, spraying), **temperature** (warm water melts grease faster) and **time** (how long the product stays on the dirt). If one force goes down, another must go up. A hotel laundry with hot water and a machine needs less chemistry than a woman washing by hand in cold borehole water.

blocks.title: The four cleaning forces
items: Chemistry: the product
Action: scrubbing or agitation
Temperature: warm water
Time: contact before rinsing
blocks.caption: Reduce one force and you must increase another to get the same clean result.

blocks.text: This matters for your labels. When you write "leave for 10 minutes before brushing" on a toilet cleaner, you are using time to do work that chemistry alone cannot do. When you advise soaking heavily soiled clothes, you are adding time. Good directions are part of the product.

**Hard water** is the other thing to know. Borehole and well water in many parts of Nigeria carry dissolved calcium and magnesium. These minerals react with anionic surfactants and waste some of their power, which is why laundry detergents contain a **builder** such as soda ash (sodium carbonate) to soften the water first.

blocks.title: Worked example: matching four complaints to four products
blocks.context: For example, Ngozi runs a small guest house in Owerri and asks you what she should buy. She lists four problems: greasy kitchen floors, yellow-brown rings in the toilets, cloudy bathroom mirrors, and towels that look grey.
steps: Greasy kitchen floor: grease needs an alkaline surfactant cleaner, so you recommend the heavy-duty floor cleaner, diluted in warm water, with a scrubbing brush (action plus temperature).
Toilet rings: the yellow-brown ring is usually mineral scale with stains, which needs acid, so you recommend the acid toilet bowl cleaner left for 10 minutes before brushing (time).
Cloudy mirrors: a light film needs very little surfactant and a fast-drying solvent, so you recommend the glass cleaner, sprayed and wiped with a dry cloth.
Grey towels: soil building up in hard water, so you recommend the liquid laundry detergent with soda ash builder, a soak before washing, and the full dose on the label.
You warn her clearly: keep the toilet cleaner and any bleach apart, and never pour one after the other into the same toilet.
blocks.result: Ngozi leaves with three bottles and one keg that each fit a real problem, plus one safety rule. A matched recommendation brings repeat orders; a single "all-purpose" product that fails on the toilet ring does not.

blocks.title: The rule you will see in every module
blocks.text: Never mix bleach (sodium hypochlorite) with an acid product such as a toilet cleaner or vinegar: it releases chlorine gas. Never mix bleach with ammonia or ammonia-containing cleaners: it releases toxic chloramine gases. Both gases harm the eyes and lungs. This is why this course makes its acid toilet cleaner and its glass cleaner without bleach or ammonia.

takeaways: Surfactants have an oil-loving end and a water-loving end; that is how grease is lifted
Grease needs alkaline products, mineral scale needs acid, germs need a disinfectant after cleaning
Chemistry, action, temperature and time work together; lower one and raise another
Anionic and cationic surfactants cancel each other, so never put BKC into LAS or SLES products
Bleach must never meet acids or ammonia

activity.title: Map the dirt in one building
steps: Choose one place you know well: your home, a church, a school or a shop.
Walk through it and list at least six cleaning problems you can see (for example, greasy cooker, toilet ring, dusty glass).
Beside each problem write the dirt type (grease, scale, film or germs) and the pH group of product that fits it.
Mark which of the six products in this course you would sell for each, and one line of directions using time, action or temperature.
activity.evidence: A photo of your handwritten dirt map with at least six rows.

lessons.title: Your raw-material store: identifying, buying and storing each chemical
objectives: Name each raw material used in this course, what it does and how it is usually sold
Ask a supplier for the right documents and read a safety data sheet
Check a delivery for the correct strength, condition and labelling
Store raw materials so that incompatible chemicals stay apart

blocks.text: Chemical markets in Nigerian cities sell everything you need, often from open drums with hand-written labels. That is where most quality problems start. A production business buys from sellers who can tell you the strength of what they sell, keeps every material in a labelled, closed container, and stores incompatible materials apart. This lesson gives you a working list of the materials in this course and how to handle each.

blocks.name: test-tube
blocks.caption: Know exactly what is in each container before it enters a batch.

head: Material
Job in your products
Usually sold as
Main hazard
rows: Main laundry and dish surfactant after neutralising
Dark brown thick liquid, about 96% active
Corrosive acid: burns skin and eyes
Corrosive alkali; heats up strongly in water
Builder: softens hard water, raises pH

blocks.text: Documents to ask for

Ask every supplier for two documents. The **safety data sheet (SDS)** is a standard 16-section sheet that lists the hazards, first aid, safe storage and what the chemical must not touch. The **certificate of analysis (COA)** states the measured strength of a particular lot, for example "active matter 96.2%" for LABSA. Big importers usually have both. If a seller has neither, buy a small amount, mark it "strength unknown" and do not base your formula on it.

On an SDS, read section 2 (hazards and pictograms), section 4 (first aid), section 7 (handling and storage) and section 10 (stability and reactivity, which lists the materials it must be kept away from). Copy the key lines into your own one-page summary and pin it in your store.
Checking a delivery

items: Check the container: closed, not leaking, not bulging, with a readable label showing the name and, ideally, the lot number.
Compare the label with your order and the COA: same material, same strength.
Look at the material: flakes should be dry and free-flowing, not wet lumps; SLES should be smooth paste, not watery.
Weigh it on your platform scale. Paying for 25 kg and receiving 23 kg is a 2 kg loss.
Write the date, supplier, lot number and weight in your raw-material book, then move it straight to its storage zone.

blocks.title: Worked example: checking a 25 kg SLES delivery
blocks.context: For example, Bisi in Ibadan orders 25 kg of SLES 70% for her dish liquid. The trader delivers a jerrycan with a hand-written label.
steps: She asks for the COA. The trader shows a photo on WhatsApp of a COA stating active matter 70.1% for a lot number that matches the original drum label. She saves the photo.
She opens the jerrycan in her ventilated store. The paste is smooth and pale. A runny, watery paste would suggest dilution.
She weighs the full jerrycan: 26.4 kg. The empty jerrycan of the same type weighs 1.4 kg, so the net SLES is 26.4 minus 1.4, which is 25.0 kg.
She writes: date, supplier name, lot number, 25.0 kg, COA saved, "accepted".
Her formula needs 2.0 kg of SLES paste per 25 kg dish batch, so 25.0 kg is enough for 25.0 / 2.0 = 12 full batches, with 1.0 kg left over.
blocks.result: Bisi knows the strength, the quantity and the number of batches she can make before she reorders. If a batch ever behaves strangely, the lot number in her book leads her back to this delivery.

blocks.text: Storing materials so they cannot meet

Group your store into three zones on separate shelves or pallets, with a clear gap between them and a label on each shelf edge. **Acids**: LABSA and citric acid. **Alkalis**: caustic soda and soda ash. **Oxidisers**: any bleach (sodium hypochlorite) you keep for cleaning or resale. Keep isopropyl alcohol and fragrances in a fourth spot away from heat, sockets and any flame. Keep powders off the floor and sealed, because caustic soda absorbs moisture from the air and goes lumpy.

blocks.title: Store zoning: who sits next to whom
items: Acids: LABSA, citric acid
Alkalis: caustic soda, soda ash
Oxidiser: bleach, alone
Flammables: IPA, fragrance
blocks.caption: Four zones with a gap between each, so a leak from one cannot reach another.

blocks.title: Never decant into food or drink containers
blocks.text: Do not store any raw material or finished product in a water bottle, soft-drink bottle or food tub. Children and adults have drunk cleaning chemicals from familiar bottles. Use proper labelled chemical containers only.

takeaways: Learn the job and hazard of every material before using it
Ask for an SDS and a COA; a material of unknown strength cannot anchor a formula
Check, weigh and record each delivery, including the lot number
Store acids, alkalis, bleach and flammables in separate zones

activity.title: Build your raw-material register
steps: Visit or call two suppliers and ask what documents they can give for LABSA, SLES and caustic soda.
Make a register page with columns: date, material, supplier, lot number, strength, net weight, documents, accepted or rejected.
For one material, find its SDS (from the supplier or the manufacturer's website) and copy sections 2, 4, 7 and 10 onto one page.
Sketch your store with the four zones marked.
activity.evidence: Your register page, the one-page SDS summary and the store sketch.

lessons.title: PPE, workshop layout and first aid for a small cleaning-products room
objectives: Choose the protective equipment needed for each task in production
Lay out a small room so materials flow one way from store to finished goods
Follow the correct order for diluting acids and caustic soda
Give correct first aid for splashes, swallowing and gas exposure

blocks.text: Most injuries in small production rooms happen during three moments: weighing concentrated chemicals, dissolving caustic soda, and pouring one liquid into another. This lesson sets up your protection, your room and your emergency response before your first real batch.

blocks.name: goggles
blocks.caption: Splash goggles are the single most important item; eyes cannot be replaced.

blocks.text: Protective equipment for each task

head: Task
Minimum protection
rows: Splash goggles, nitrile or thick rubber gloves, long sleeves, closed shoes, apron
Splash goggles, gloves, apron, long sleeves
Handling powders (soda ash, citric acid, CMC)
Gloves and safety glasses or goggles
Gloves, goggles, no flames or smoking anywhere near

blocks.text: Ordinary sunglasses and prescription glasses do not protect against splashes from the side. Choose closed splash goggles. Tie back long hair and do not wear loose wrappers that can dip into a drum.
Laying out the room

Arrange your room so materials move in one direction: from the store, to weighing, to mixing, to filling, to the finished-goods shelf. Nobody should carry a bucket of concentrated chemical back past someone filling bottles. Keep the mixing area near a tap or a large drum of clean water, and near a window or door for air.

blocks.title: One-way flow through the room
items: Raw-material store
Weighing bench
Mixing drums
Resting and testing
Filling and labelling
Finished-goods shelf
blocks.caption: Materials only move forward, which keeps concentrates away from finished bottles and people.

blocks.title: Worked example: setting up a 3 m by 4 m room
blocks.context: For example, Hauwa in Kaduna rents a single room behind her shop, 3 metres by 4 metres, with one door and one window, to make laundry detergent and dish liquid.
steps: She puts the raw-material shelves on the wall farthest from the door, in four labelled zones, with acids at one end and bleach at the other.
Next to the shelves she places a sturdy table for the scale, so weighing happens beside the store.
She puts two 50-litre plastic mixing drums under the window, so fumes and dust move outside.
Near the door she sets a filling table and the finished-goods shelf, so bottles leave without passing the mixing drums.
Beside the mixing drums she keeps a 25-litre jerrycan of clean water with a tap, a clean eye-wash bottle, and a bucket of sand with a scoop for spills.
She pins the SDS summaries and the first-aid steps on the wall at eye level, and keeps children and customers out of the room.
blocks.result: Hauwa's room has a clear path from store to door, water within reach of every splash point, and no reason for concentrates to travel past finished products.

blocks.text: Order of addition: the rules that prevent boiling and splashing

items: **Caustic soda goes into water, slowly**, never water onto caustic soda. It heats up strongly as it dissolves. Use cold water in a heat-resistant plastic container, never aluminium, which caustic soda attacks.
**LABSA goes into water**, stirring, not water into a small pool of LABSA.
**Add the caustic solution to the diluted acid slowly**, in portions, and wait between portions. Neutralising produces heat.
**Never pour a bleach product into the same container, drain or toilet** as an acid product or any ammonia product.
Label every bucket with what is in it, even if it is only for an hour.

blocks.title: First aid you must know before you start
blocks.text: Eyes: rinse immediately with gently running clean water for at least 15 minutes, holding the eyelids open, then go to a clinic with the product label. Skin: remove contaminated clothing and rinse with plenty of running water for at least 15 minutes. Swallowed: do not make the person vomit; rinse the mouth, and get medical help at once, taking the container or label. Gas from mixed products: leave the room for fresh air at once, open doors and windows only if it is safe, and get medical help for coughing, burning or breathing difficulty. Do not use vinegar or other chemicals to "neutralise" a splash on skin or eyes.
Spills and waste

For a small liquid spill, stop the source, cover the spill with dry sand, scoop it into a labelled bucket and wash the area with plenty of water. For a caustic soda flake spill, sweep it up dry before adding any water. Rinse water from cleaning drums contains surfactant: use it to wash the room floor rather than pouring large amounts into a gutter. Never pour concentrates down a drain or onto soil.

Because you will store isopropyl alcohol and fragrances, keep a working fire extinguisher by the door, learn how to use it, and keep electrical sockets dry and away from the mixing drums. Lock the room when you leave it. A production room is a workplace, not a store room that children can wander into.

blocks.title: Keep a near-miss book
blocks.text: Write down every splash, spill or near-miss, what caused it and what you changed. A pattern of small events is the warning before a serious one.

takeaways: Splash goggles and gloves are compulsory whenever concentrates are open
Set the room so materials flow one way, with water beside every splash point
Caustic soda and LABSA both go into water, slowly
Rinse eyes and skin with running water for at least 15 minutes; never induce vomiting
Bleach must never share a container, drain or toilet with acids or ammonia

activity.title: Set up and photograph your safety station
steps: Collect splash goggles, gloves, an apron, a dust mask, a water container with a tap or eye-wash bottle, and a bucket of sand.
Draw your room layout showing the one-way flow from store to finished goods.
Write the first-aid steps in large letters on one sheet and pin it next to the mixing area.
Practise putting on your full PPE in under one minute.
activity.evidence: A photo of your safety station with PPE and the pinned first-aid sheet, plus your room sketch.

quiz.q: A customer's kitchen floor is covered with old cooking grease. Which product type should you recommend?
options: The alkaline heavy-duty floor cleaner in warm water with scrubbing
Plain cold water left to soak
quiz.explain: Grease responds to alkaline surfactant cleaners, helped by warm water (temperature) and scrubbing (action).

quiz.q: Amaka wants to make her dish liquid "also kill germs" by adding BKC to it. What will happen?
options: It will become a strong disinfecting dish liquid
The anionic surfactants and cationic BKC will react and weaken both
Nothing, the two ignore each other
It will become thicker and better
quiz.explain: LAS and SLES are anionic; BKC is cationic. Opposite charges combine into a cloudy complex and both lose their effect.

quiz.q: A trader offers cheap LABSA but has no COA and does not know its strength. What is the best action?
options: Buy a full drum because it is cheap
Assume it is 96% and use it in your standard formula
Buy only a small amount, mark it "strength unknown" and do not base a formula on it
Dilute it with water to make it safer
quiz.explain: Your caustic soda calculation depends on the LABSA strength. Unknown strength means unreliable batches.

quiz.q: Which storage plan is correct?
options: Bleach on the same shelf as citric acid to save space
Caustic soda flakes open on the floor
Isopropyl alcohol next to the gas cooker
Acids, alkalis, bleach and flammables in separate zones with gaps between them
quiz.explain: Separate zones stop a leak or a mistake from bringing incompatible chemicals together.

quiz.q: Caustic solution splashes into Kemi's eye. What should happen first?
options: Rinse with running clean water for at least 15 minutes, holding the eyelid open
Put a drop of vinegar in the eye
Wipe it with a cloth and continue working
Wait to see if it starts to hurt
quiz.explain: Immediate, long rinsing with water is the correct first aid. Then go to a clinic with the label.

quiz.q: When dissolving caustic soda flakes, which is correct?
options: Pour water onto the flakes in an aluminium pot
Add flakes slowly into cold water in a heat-resistant plastic container
Add flakes into hot LABSA directly
Dissolve them in a closed room
quiz.explain: Caustic soda goes into water slowly. It heats up as it dissolves and attacks aluminium.

modules.title: Production Runs: Laundry Detergent, Dish Liquid and Floor Cleaner
modules.overview: You will run three full production batches from a written formula: a 20 kg liquid laundry detergent built on neutralised sulphonic acid, a 25 kg dishwashing liquid filled by weight into 500 ml bottles, and a 20 kg floor cleaner concentrate with tested dilution directions. Each lesson works from percentages to kilograms, so you can scale any batch up or down.

lessons.title: Liquid laundry detergent: neutralising sulphonic acid in a 20 kg batch
objectives: Convert a percentage formula into kilograms for any batch size
Calculate the caustic soda needed to neutralise LABSA and finish the job by pH
Run the mixing steps in the correct order with full safety
Record a laundry batch so the next one comes out the same

blocks.text: Liquid laundry detergent is the product most small producers start with because demand is steady: homes, laundries, hostels and schools all wash clothes every week. The method below uses **LABSA** (sulphonic acid), which becomes a strong cleaning surfactant called **LAS** once it is neutralised with caustic soda, plus SLES for foam and soda ash to soften hard water.

blocks.name: bucket
blocks.caption: Laundry detergent is mixed in clean plastic drums or buckets, never in aluminium.

blocks.text: The starting formula

Formulas are written in **percent by weight**, so they work for any batch size. To find the weight of each ingredient, multiply the batch weight by the percentage. This is a starting formula for you to test and adjust, not a fixed standard.

head: Ingredient
% by weight
In a 20 kg batch
rows: to bring the total to 20 kg

blocks.text: How much caustic soda?

One molecule of sulphonic acid reacts with one molecule of sodium hydroxide. Using their molecular weights (about 326 for the acid and 40 for sodium hydroxide), 1 kg of pure acid needs about 0.123 kg of caustic soda. For 96% LABSA, that becomes about 0.118 kg per kg. Commercial LABSA also contains a little free sulphuric acid, so you usually need slightly more. That is why you **calculate first, add about 90% of the calculation, then finish slowly by measuring pH**.

blocks.title: Worked example: the numbers for a 20 kg laundry batch
blocks.context: For example, Chiamaka in Onitsha supplies two laundries and wants a 20 kg batch of the formula above. Her LABSA COA says 96%.
steps: LABSA: 20 kg x 8% = 1.60 kg.
Caustic soda by calculation: 1.60 x 0.118 = about 0.19 kg (189 g).
First addition, about 90%: 189 x 0.9 = about 170 g. She dissolves 190 g of flakes in 1.7 kg of cold water to make a roughly 10% solution, and adds it in portions.
SLES: 20 x 6% = 1.20 kg. Soda ash: 20 x 1% = 0.20 kg. CMC: 20 x 0.3% = 60 g.

Fixed ingredients so far: 1.60 + 0.19 + 1.20 + 0.20 + 0.06 = 3.25 kg. Water (including the water used for the caustic solution) is about 20 minus 3.25, which is 16.75 kg, minus any salt, fragrance and colour she adds.
blocks.result: Chiamaka's batch sheet lists every weight before she opens a single container. She will record the actual caustic used, because her finishing pH decides the final figure.

blocks.text: Production steps in order

items: Put on goggles, gloves, apron and long sleeves. Open the window.
Weigh about 12 kg of clean water into a 30 to 50 litre plastic drum.
Pour in the 1.60 kg of LABSA slowly while stirring with a long plastic or wooden paddle. The liquid turns cloudy brown.
In a separate labelled jug, dissolve the caustic soda flakes into cold water (flakes into water, never the reverse).
Add the caustic solution to the drum in four or five portions, stirring and waiting a few minutes between portions. The drum gets warm.
After about 90% of the calculated caustic, test the pH with a strip. Keep adding small amounts and testing until the pH is about 7 to 8. The liquid usually becomes clearer as it neutralises.
Dissolve the soda ash in a little warm water and stir it in. Adding soda ash only after neutralising avoids fizzing.
Sprinkle the CMC slowly onto the moving liquid, or premix it with a little SLES, to avoid lumps.
Add the SLES, pre-softened in some of the water, and stir gently to avoid excess foam.
Add colour, fragrance and preservative. Make up to 20 kg with water. Add salt solution in small steps only if you want it thicker.
Cover and rest overnight so foam and air bubbles rise out, then check pH (aim for about 9 to 10 after the soda ash) and fill.

blocks.title: Laundry batch order of addition
items: Water in drum
LABSA into water
Caustic solution in portions
Check pH 7 to 8
Soda ash, CMC, SLES
Top up, rest, fill
blocks.caption: Neutralise first, then add the builder and other ingredients.

blocks.title: Two corrosives in one drum
blocks.text: LABSA is a strong acid and caustic soda is a strong alkali. Both burn skin and eyes, and the reaction between them produces heat. Never rush the caustic additions, never lean over the drum while pouring, and keep your eye-wash water within reach.
If the pH goes too high

If you overshoot and the pH reaches 9 or more before the soda ash, stop adding caustic. Stir in a very small amount of extra LABSA (for example 20 g at a time, poured into the drum, not the other way round), wait, and test again. Record exactly what you added. A product that is too alkaline is harsh on hands that wash clothes by hand.

Write the batch record as you go: date, batch number, every weight, the pH after each caustic portion, the final pH, the appearance and the final weight. Your next batch starts from this record, not from memory.

blocks.title: Why CMC?
blocks.text: CMC (sodium carboxymethyl cellulose) helps stop loosened dirt from settling back on the fabric during the wash. It is one reason white clothes stay white rather than slowly turning grey.

takeaways: Multiply batch weight by percentage to get each ingredient's weight
About 0.118 kg of caustic soda neutralises 1 kg of 96% LABSA; finish by pH
Order: water, LABSA, caustic in portions, pH check, then soda ash, CMC and SLES
Rest the batch overnight before filling and record every figure

activity.title: Run a 2 kg laundry test batch
steps: Scale the formula to 2 kg and write the full batch sheet before starting.
Wearing full PPE, run the steps in order, testing pH after each caustic portion.
Record the actual caustic used and the final pH after soda ash.
Wash two identical soiled cloths, one with your product and one with a shop brand, at the same dose, and compare.
activity.evidence: Your completed batch sheet with pH readings and a photo of the two washed cloths side by side.

lessons.title: Dishwashing liquid: a 25 kg production run filled by weight
objectives: Adapt the laundry chemistry into a milder, neutral dishwashing liquid
Thicken a batch with salt using a recorded step method
Measure density and calculate the correct fill weight for a 500 ml bottle
Work out how many bottles a batch will fill and plan packaging to match

blocks.text: Dishwashing liquid sells in large volumes to homes, food sellers and restaurants. Hands spend a long time in it, so it must be **near neutral** (pH about 6 to 8), with no soda ash. It also needs to look rich: clear, evenly coloured and thick enough to pour slowly. This lesson takes you from a 1 kg test to a 25 kg production run and through the step most beginners get wrong: filling by weight.

blocks.name: sponge
blocks.caption: A good dish liquid lifts grease quickly and stays gentle on hands.

blocks.text: The neutralisation follows the same steps as Lesson 2.1: LABSA into water, caustic solution in portions, testing as you go. The difference is the end point. You stop at about pH 7 and add no soda ash. Then you add the SLES and thicken.
Thickening with salt, the controlled way

Salt thickens LAS and SLES blends up to a point. Past that point, the liquid becomes thin again and you cannot take the salt back out. So you never pour salt in by guesswork. Make a **25% salt solution** (250 g of salt dissolved in 750 g of water). Add it 100 g at a time, stir for two minutes, and check thickness each time by timing how long a fixed amount takes to flow, for example 100 ml through a funnel.

blocks.title: Worked example: salt steps on a 25 kg batch
blocks.context: For example, Funke in Abeokuta has neutralised her 25 kg dish batch to pH 7 and added the SLES. It flows like water. She times 100 ml through a plastic funnel after each 100 g of 25% salt solution.
steps: Start: 4 seconds.
After 100 g: 6 seconds. After 200 g: 9 seconds. After 300 g: 14 seconds.
After 400 g: 19 seconds. After 500 g: 22 seconds.
After 600 g: 21 seconds. The time has dropped, so she has passed the peak. She stops.
Total salt solution added: 600 g, which contains 600 x 0.25 = 150 g of salt, which is 0.6% of the batch.
She writes on her formula: "next time, add 500 g of 25% salt solution, then check".
blocks.result: Funke's batch is slightly past its peak but still thick. Her next batch will stop at 500 g, and her record shows exactly why.

blocks.title: Salt curve: thicker, then thinner
items: No salt: thin
Small steps: thickening
Peak thickness: stop
Too much: thins again
blocks.caption: Add salt in measured steps and stop when the flow time stops rising.

blocks.text: Filling by weight, not by eye

Your label promises a volume, such as 500 ml. Most scales measure weight, and dish liquid is a little heavier than water. To find the right fill weight, measure the **density**: weigh an empty measuring jug, fill it exactly to the 1 litre mark, weigh again and subtract. If 1 litre weighs 1,030 g, the density is 1.03 g per ml.

blocks.title: Worked example: fill weight and bottle count
blocks.context: For example, Funke's finished 25 kg batch measures 1,030 g per litre. She sells in 500 ml bottles.
steps: Fill weight per bottle: 500 ml x 1.03 g/ml = 515 g of product.
Bottles from the batch: 25,000 g / 515 g = 48.5, so 48 full bottles.
Leftover: 25,000 minus (48 x 515) = 25,000 minus 24,720 = 280 g, which she keeps as her retained sample and for testing.
She tares (zeros) the scale with an empty bottle and cap on it, then fills each bottle to 515 g.
She checks every tenth bottle again and writes the reading in her record.
blocks.result: Funke buys exactly 48 bottles, caps and labels for each 25 kg batch, every customer receives what the label says, and she has a sample to look at if anyone complains.

blocks.text: Production-day checklist

items: Bottles washed with clean water and fully dry, caps counted, labels printed with the batch number before filling starts.
Batch rested overnight so foam has risen and the liquid is clear.
Fill using a funnel or a drum tap, never by dipping bottles into the drum.
Wipe each bottle, cap it tightly, label it, and place it on the finished-goods shelf in batch order.

blocks.title: No formalin
blocks.text: Some local recipes add formalin (formaldehyde solution) as a preservative. Formaldehyde is classified as a cancer-causing substance by the International Agency for Research on Cancer, and dish liquid touches hands and plates. Use a preservative sold for this purpose at the supplier's stated rate.

blocks.title: Clear liquid sells better
blocks.text: If your batch looks hazy, check the pH first. Haze often means it is not fully neutralised or has too much salt. Fix the cause, then record it on your formula.

takeaways: Dish liquid stops at about pH 7 with no soda ash, to stay gentle on hands
Add 25% salt solution in measured steps and stop when the flow time stops rising
Fill weight equals label volume times measured density
Count bottles, caps and labels from the batch weight before you buy packaging

activity.title: Measure, thicken and fill
steps: Make a 2 kg dish test batch and neutralise it to about pH 7.
Add 25% salt solution in 10 g steps, timing 100 ml through a funnel after each step, and record the curve.
Measure the density by weighing exactly 1 litre (or 500 ml and doubling).
Calculate the fill weight for a 500 ml bottle and fill two bottles by weight.
activity.evidence: Your salt curve table, density calculation and a photo of the two filled bottles on the scale.

lessons.title: Heavy-duty floor cleaner concentrate and the dilution ladder test
objectives: Make a 20 kg alkaline floor cleaner concentrate with a nonionic and anionic blend
Run a dilution ladder test to find the lowest dose that cleans well
Write clear dilution directions that a cleaner can follow with a bucket
Warn customers about surfaces the product must not be used on

blocks.text: Floor cleaner is a **concentrate**: the customer adds a small amount to a bucket of water. That means your directions matter as much as your formula. A good concentrate with a vague dose ("add some") either wastes product or leaves floors greasy, and the customer blames the product. In this lesson you make the concentrate, then test it to find the right dose.

blocks.name: broom
blocks.caption: Floors are swept first; the floor cleaner then removes the greasy film that sweeping leaves behind.

head: Ingredient
% by weight
In a 20 kg batch
Job
rows: Cuts oily soil, helps dissolve fragrance
Raises pH, attacks grease, softens water

blocks.text: Making the concentrate

items: Wear goggles, gloves and a dust mask for the soda ash.
Weigh about 14 kg of water into the drum. Dissolve the 0.60 kg of soda ash in it, stirring until no grains remain. The water warms slightly.
Soften the 1.40 kg of SLES in a little of the water and stir it in gently.
Mix the fragrance into the AEO-9 first, then add this premix to the drum. The nonionic surfactant helps the oily fragrance stay dissolved instead of floating.
Add colour and preservative, make up to 20 kg with water and stir.
Rest overnight. Check that the liquid is uniform with no oily layer on top, and record the pH (expect strongly alkaline, roughly 10 to 11).

blocks.title: If fragrance floats
blocks.text: An oily ring on top means the fragrance is not fully dissolved. Next time, increase the AEO-9 slightly or reduce the fragrance, and always premix fragrance with the nonionic before adding it.
The dilution ladder test

A **dilution ladder** tests the same concentrate at several strengths on the same kind of dirt, so the result comes from evidence, not guesswork. You need a few buckets, a measuring cylinder or syringe, identical mops or cloths, and a greasy floor area divided into equal patches.

blocks.title: Dilution ladder: strongest to weakest
items: 1 in 50: 100 ml per 5 L
1 in 100: 50 ml per 5 L
1 in 200: 25 ml per 5 L
Water only: control
blocks.caption: Choose the weakest rung that still cleans well; that is your label dose.

blocks.title: Worked example: finding the dose for a restaurant kitchen
blocks.context: For example, Rukayat in Ilorin wants to sell her concentrate to a busy buka (local restaurant) with a greasy tiled kitchen floor. She tests on four equal patches, each about 1 metre square, using a 5 litre bucket per patch.
steps: Patch A, water only: still slippery and dull after mopping.
Patch B, 1 in 200 (25 ml in 5 L): better, but a slight slippery film remains near the stove.
Patch C, 1 in 100 (50 ml in 5 L): no film, dries without streaks.
Patch D, 1 in 50 (100 ml in 5 L): also clean, but no better than C and leaves some foam to rinse.
She chooses 1 in 100 for kitchens and writes 1 in 200 for light daily cleaning of living areas.
From a 4 litre keg at 50 ml per bucket: 4,000 / 50 = 80 buckets for kitchen use.
blocks.result: Rukayat's label reads: "Kitchens: 50 ml (about 2 capfuls of a 25 ml cap) per 5 litre bucket. Light daily cleaning: 25 ml per 5 litre bucket." The buka manager can see the keg lasts 80 kitchen buckets, which helps her sell it.

blocks.text: Writing directions people actually follow

items: Give the dose in a measure the customer owns: a cap of known size, a tablespoon, or millilitres per bucket.
State the bucket size: 5 litres, 10 litres or a standard paint bucket.
Say when to rinse: on heavy grease, rinse after mopping to avoid a sticky film.
Say what not to do: do not mix with bleach or other cleaners in the bucket.

blocks.title: Surfaces to avoid
blocks.text: Strong alkaline cleaners can dull or damage waxed or varnished wooden floors and some painted surfaces, and alkalis attack aluminium. Tell customers to test on a small hidden area first and to keep the concentrate in its own plastic container. Keep the concentrate away from children: at full strength it irritates eyes and skin.

Finally, decide which customers need which strength. Offices with light dirt may be happy with the 1 in 200 rate; mechanic workshops and restaurant kitchens may need 1 in 50 plus scrubbing. A short dosing chart on the keg, or on a WhatsApp image you send with each delivery, saves product and keeps customers satisfied.

Pack the concentrate in sturdy HDPE (high-density polyethylene) kegs with tight screw caps, and, if you can, supply a measuring cap whose size matches your directions. A keg with a 25 ml cap and the words "2 caps per 5 litre bucket" is far easier to use correctly than a keg with no measure at all. Record the batch number on every keg so a complaint can be traced back to your batch sheet.

takeaways: Floor cleaner is a concentrate; the dose on the label is part of the product
Premix fragrance with the nonionic surfactant so it does not float
A dilution ladder finds the weakest dose that still cleans well
Directions need a dose, a bucket size, rinse advice and a no-mixing warning

activity.title: Run your own dilution ladder
steps: Make a 2 kg test batch of the floor concentrate.
Choose a greasy floor area and mark four equal patches.
Clean each with water only, 1 in 200, 1 in 100 and 1 in 50, using the same mop technique.
Photograph each patch after drying and choose your label dose.
Write the full directions for your label in plain words.
activity.evidence: Four labelled photos of the patches and your written label directions.

quiz.q: Using the course formula, how much LABSA goes into a 30 kg laundry batch at 8%?
Chiamaka has added about 90% of her calculated caustic soda to the LABSA. What should she do next?
options: Add the remaining caustic all at once
Test the pH and add small amounts until it reaches about 7 to 8
quiz.explain: LABSA strength and free acid vary, so the last part of neutralising is done in small steps guided by pH.

quiz.q: Funke's dish liquid flow times after salt steps are 14, 19, 22, then 21 seconds. What does the last reading tell her?
options: She has passed the peak thickness and should stop adding salt
quiz.explain: When the flow time falls after rising, the salt curve has passed its peak. More salt would make it thinner.

quiz.q: A dish liquid weighs 1,040 g per litre. What is the fill weight for a 750 ml bottle?
Why does the dish liquid formula leave out soda ash?
options: Dish liquid should stay near neutral so it is gentle on hands
quiz.explain: Hands spend a long time in dish water, so the product is kept at about pH 6 to 8.

quiz.q: In a dilution ladder, 1 in 100 and 1 in 50 both clean a floor equally well. Which dose should go on the label?
options: 1 in 100, the weakest dose that works
quiz.explain: The label dose is the weakest rung that still cleans well. Stronger wastes product and needs more rinsing.

quiz.q: An oily ring floats on top of Rukayat's floor cleaner after resting. What is the most likely fix?
options: Premix the fragrance with the nonionic surfactant, or use slightly more nonionic
quiz.explain: The nonionic surfactant helps dissolve the oily fragrance. Premixing them prevents separation.

modules.title: Specialist Products: Toilet Cleaner, Glass and Surface Sprays, Disinfectant Cleaner
modules.overview: These three products each carry a specific hazard: an acid, a flammable solvent and a disinfectant concentrate. You will make a citric acid toilet gel without hydrochloric acid or bleach, an ammonia-free glass cleaner and multi-surface spray, and a BKC disinfectant cleaner, and you will learn which claims you can honestly make for each.

lessons.title: Acid toilet bowl gel with citric acid: a safer descaler
objectives: Explain why toilet scale needs an acid and why this course avoids hydrochloric acid
Make a 10 kg citric acid toilet gel thickened with xanthan gum
Choose the right bottle and write the no-mixing warning correctly
Calculate fill weight and bottle count for an angled-neck bottle

blocks.text: The brown-yellow ring in a toilet bowl is mostly mineral scale from hard water and urine, with stains trapped inside it. Surfactants alone cannot remove it. It needs an **acid**, which dissolves the mineral, plus **time** in contact with the bowl. A thick gel clings to the sloping sides of the bowl, giving the acid that time.

blocks.name: toilet
blocks.caption: The gel is squeezed under the rim so it runs slowly down and clings to the scale.

blocks.text: Why citric acid, not hydrochloric acid

Many strong toilet cleaners on the market use **hydrochloric acid** ("spirit of salt"). It works fast but gives off corrosive fumes, burns skin badly, eats metal fittings and some surfaces, and is extremely dangerous if a user pours bleach into the same bowl. This course uses **citric acid**, a solid acid that is far easier to handle in a small workshop. It works more slowly, which you manage with clear directions about contact time.
SLES is not used here because it slowly breaks down in strongly acidic products. A nonionic surfactant such as AEO-9 stays stable in acid.
Making the gel

items: Wear goggles and gloves. Citric acid dust stings eyes.
Weigh about 8.5 kg of water into a clean plastic drum.
In a small cup, stir the 50 g of xanthan gum into the 100 g of glycerine to make a smooth slurry with no dry powder.
Pour the slurry into the water while stirring hard. Keep stirring for 10 to 15 minutes until it thickens and no lumps remain.
Add the 1.00 kg of citric acid slowly, stirring until all crystals dissolve.
Add the AEO-9, then colour and fragrance. Make up to 10 kg with water and stir slowly to avoid trapping air.
Rest overnight so bubbles rise. Check pH (expect about 2) and record it with the batch.

blocks.title: Hydrochloric acid cleaner vs citric acid gel
items: Hydrochloric acid cleaner
Citric acid gel
blocks.caption: The citric gel trades some speed for much safer production and use.

blocks.title: Worked example: packing a 10 kg batch
blocks.context: For example, Blessing in Port Harcourt makes the 10 kg batch for a cleaning company that services offices. She uses 750 ml angled-neck HDPE bottles with child-resistant caps.
steps: She weighs exactly 1 litre of finished gel: 1,040 g, so the density is 1.04 g per ml.
Fill weight: 750 x 1.04 = 780 g per bottle.
Bottles: 10,000 / 780 = 12.8, so 12 full bottles.
Leftover: 10,000 minus (12 x 780) = 10,000 minus 9,360 = 640 g, kept as a retained sample and for her shelf-stability test.
Each label carries the directions and the warning panel before filling starts.
blocks.result: Blessing delivers 12 identical bottles, each with a batch number, and keeps 640 g to check the gel's thickness and colour over the next month.

blocks.text: Directions and the warning panel

Write directions that use time instead of strength: "Lift the seat. Squeeze the gel under the rim all round. Leave for at least 10 minutes, or overnight for heavy scale. Brush, then flush." Repeat use breaks down old scale gradually.

blocks.title: The warning every toilet cleaner label needs
blocks.text: Print clearly: "Do not use with bleach or other cleaning products. Dangerous gas can be released." Acid plus bleach releases chlorine gas, and toilets are small, closed rooms. Also print: keep out of reach of children; avoid contact with eyes; if in eyes, rinse with water for 15 minutes and get medical advice; if swallowed, do not induce vomiting, get medical help and show the label.

blocks.title: Not for marble or terrazzo
blocks.text: Acids etch natural stone such as marble and terrazzo, and can dull some enamel finishes. Tell customers to keep the gel inside the toilet bowl and wipe up any drips on the floor straight away.

Watch your retained sample for the first month. Check once a week that the gel is still as thick as on day one, that the colour has not faded and that no crystals have formed at the bottom. Store finished bottles out of direct sun, which fades many dyes. If the gel thins over time, try slightly more xanthan gum in the next batch and note the change on your formula sheet, so every batch you sell behaves the same on the shelf and in the bowl.
Use HDPE bottles: citric acid will not attack them. Avoid metal caps and metal funnels. A child-resistant cap is strongly recommended for any acid product sold to homes.

takeaways: Toilet scale needs an acid plus contact time; a gel clings to give that time
Citric acid is far safer to handle than hydrochloric acid
Use a nonionic surfactant in acid products; SLES breaks down there
Every toilet cleaner label must warn: do not use with bleach

activity.title: Make and test a 1 kg toilet gel
steps: Scale the formula to 1 kg and write the batch sheet.
Make the gel, checking for lumps after the xanthan step.
Apply it to a scaled toilet or a kettle with limescale, leave for 10 minutes and 1 hour, then brush or rinse and photograph both results.
Draft a complete label warning panel.
activity.evidence: Batch sheet, before and after photos at both contact times, and your warning panel text.

lessons.title: Streak-free glass cleaner and multi-surface spray without ammonia
objectives: Explain why glass cleaner needs very little surfactant and soft water
Make a 10 kg glass cleaner and a 10 kg multi-surface spray
Handle isopropyl alcohol safely as a flammable liquid
Fill trigger spray bottles accurately and check spray performance

blocks.text: Glass cleaner is the opposite of floor cleaner. Glass shows every streak, and streaks come from three things: too much surfactant, minerals in the water, and slow drying. So a good glass cleaner uses **very little surfactant**, **soft water** and **a fast-drying alcohol**. Many commercial glass cleaners also contain ammonia. This course leaves ammonia out, because a customer who later sprays a bleach product on the same surface could release toxic chloramine gas.

blocks.name: window
blocks.caption: Windows and mirrors show every streak, so less product does more.

blocks.text: Water quality decides the result

Borehole and tap water contain dissolved minerals. When the water evaporates from glass, the minerals stay behind as spots. Use **distilled or deionised water** for glass cleaner, for example water sold for batteries or laboratories. Test it simply: let a few drops dry on a clean mirror. Good water leaves no ring.

blocks.title: Glass cleaner vs multi-surface spray
items: Glass cleaner
Multi-surface spray
blocks.caption: Same production line, two different balances of surfactant and alcohol.

blocks.text: Making both products

items: Switch off any flame, stove or generator nearby. No smoking. Open the window and door.
Weigh the distilled water into a clean, rinsed drum (rinse with distilled water too, so tap minerals are not left behind).
For glass cleaner: dissolve the 30 g of SLES in a cup of the water first, then stir it in gently.
Add the isopropyl alcohol last, pouring slowly close to the liquid surface, and close the IPA container immediately.
For the multi-surface spray: premix fragrance into the AEO-9, add it with the SLES, then add the IPA.
Stir gently, cover, and fill the same day into labelled trigger bottles.

blocks.title: Isopropyl alcohol is highly flammable
blocks.text: Its vapour can catch fire from a flame or spark some distance away. Store it in a closed container away from heat and sunlight, measure it only in a ventilated room with no flames, and keep a fire extinguisher by the door. The finished glass cleaner label should also say: keep away from flames and heat.

blocks.title: Worked example: filling an office order
blocks.context: For example, Zainab in Abuja wins an order for 18 glass cleaners and 18 multi-surface sprays in 500 ml trigger bottles for an office block. She measures the glass cleaner at 985 g per litre (alcohol makes it lighter than water) and the multi-surface spray at 995 g per litre.
steps: Glass cleaner fill weight: 500 x 0.985 = 492.5 g, rounded to 493 g.
Glass cleaner needed: 18 x 493 = 8,874 g, so a 10 kg batch is enough with about 1.1 kg spare.
Multi-surface fill weight: 500 x 0.995 = 497.5 g, rounded to 498 g.
Multi-surface needed: 18 x 498 = 8,964 g, also covered by a 10 kg batch with about 1.0 kg spare.
She tests each trigger: 10 pulls into a cup should give an even mist, not a jet or drips. She replaces any faulty trigger before delivery.
blocks.result: Zainab makes one 10 kg batch of each, fills 36 bottles by weight, keeps the spare as retained samples and refills for the office's next order.

blocks.text: Testing for streaks

Clean half of a mirror with your glass cleaner and the other half with a shop brand, using the same lint-free cloth technique. Look at both halves in daylight from an angle. If yours streaks, reduce the SLES (try 0.2%) or check your water. If it dries too slowly, the alcohol level may be low. Change one thing at a time and record each test.

blocks.title: Sell the cloth with the spray
blocks.text: Many streaks come from dirty or fluffy cloths. Offering a microfibre cloth with an office starter pack improves results and makes your product look better.

Offices and cleaning companies use these sprays quickly, so offer a **refill pack**: a 4 litre HDPE keg of the same product, with the same batch number system, that the cleaner uses to refill the trigger bottles. Refills cost you less in packaging, give the customer a better price per litre, and bring you back every month. Label the keg with the same directions and warnings as the bottle, and remind cleaners to rinse a trigger bottle before refilling it with a different product, so glass cleaner and multi-surface spray never mix.

Tell customers to test the multi-surface spray on a hidden spot of painted, varnished or plastic surfaces first, because alcohol can affect some finishes. Neither product is a disinfectant; do not describe them as "germ-killing" on the label.

takeaways: Streaks come from too much surfactant, hard water or slow drying
Use distilled or deionised water and very little SLES for glass
Leave out ammonia, so no customer can create chloramine gas by mixing with bleach
Isopropyl alcohol is highly flammable: no flames, good ventilation, closed containers

activity.title: Half-mirror streak test
steps: Make 500 g of glass cleaner with distilled water and 500 g with tap water.
Clean one half of a mirror with each, using the same cloth technique.
Photograph both halves in daylight at an angle.
Repeat with 0.2% SLES if you see streaks, and record which version wins.
activity.evidence: Photos of the mirror test and a short note of which water and surfactant level gave no streaks.

lessons.title: BKC disinfectant cleaner: production, compatibility and honest claims
objectives: Explain the difference between cleaning and disinfecting
Make a ready-to-use BKC disinfectant cleaner from a 50% concentrate using the supplier's in-use level
Prove the BKC and anionic incompatibility with a jar test
Write claims and directions you can stand behind, and know when registration is needed

blocks.text: **Cleaning** removes dirt. **Disinfecting** kills germs on a surface. Disinfectants work much better on a surface that has already been cleaned, because dirt shields germs and uses up the active ingredient. That is why the directions for any disinfectant start with "clean first". In this lesson you make a disinfectant cleaner based on **benzalkonium chloride (BKC)**, a quaternary ammonium compound ("quat") widely used in hard-surface disinfectants.

blocks.name: shield
blocks.caption: A disinfectant protects only when used at the right strength, on a clean surface, for the right contact time.

blocks.text: Your supplier's sheet sets the numbers

BKC is usually sold as a **50% concentrate**. The level of BKC needed in your finished product, and the contact time needed to kill germs, depend on the grade of BKC and the germs you are targeting. Do not take these figures from social media. Use the in-use level and contact time stated on your supplier's technical data sheet for a hard-surface disinfectant, and write them into your batch sheet.

blocks.title: BKC 50% is corrosive
blocks.text: The concentrate can burn skin and cause serious eye damage. Wear splash goggles, gloves and an apron, weigh it in a ventilated room, and always add the concentrate to water. The diluted finished product is much milder but still needs the warning panel.

blocks.title: Worked example: a 20 kg ready-to-use batch
blocks.context: For example, Adaeze in Enugu buys BKC 50%. Her supplier's technical sheet gives an in-use level of 0.2% active BKC for hard surfaces with a 10-minute contact time. (Your own sheet may give a different figure: always use yours.)
steps: Active BKC needed: 20 kg x 0.2% = 0.04 kg (40 g).
Concentrate needed: 40 g / 0.50 = 80 g of BKC 50%.
Nonionic surfactant for cleaning power: AEO-9 at 1%, so 20 x 1% = 200 g.
Fragrance at 0.3%: 60 g, premixed into the AEO-9.
She weighs the water, stirs in the AEO-9 and fragrance premix, then adds the 80 g of BKC 50% last, slowly, and stirs.
blocks.result: Adaeze's 20 kg batch contains 0.2% BKC as her supplier specifies, and her label states the 10-minute contact time from the same sheet.

blocks.text: The jar test: why BKC stays away from anionics

Pour 100 ml of your finished disinfectant cleaner into a clear jar. Add a few drops of your dish liquid (which contains LAS and SLES) and stir. The liquid usually turns cloudy as the positively charged BKC and the negatively charged anionic surfactants grab each other. The BKC tied up in that cloud is no longer free to work on germs. This is why your disinfectant uses a nonionic surfactant only, why you clean the drum thoroughly between a dish batch and a disinfectant batch, and why your directions say to rinse soapy residues before disinfecting.

blocks.title: Before you put "disinfectant" on a label
items: Active level from supplier sheet
Contact time stated in directions
Clean first, then disinfect
No anionic surfactants in formula
Registration route checked with NAFDAC
blocks.caption: Each item must be true before the word disinfectant appears on your product.

blocks.text: Honest claims

items: Do not print "kills 99.9% of germs" or name specific germs unless your product has been tested for that claim. That figure comes from laboratory testing, not from the formula.
Do not suggest the product protects people from any disease, or that it can be used on skin, in wounds or on food.
Do print the directions: clean the surface, apply undiluted, leave wet for the stated contact time, then wipe or rinse food-contact surfaces with clean water.
Do print the warning panel: keep out of reach of children, avoid eyes, do not mix with other products, first aid, and your batch number.

blocks.text: NAFDAC's MSME page lists the simple products that micro and small businesses can register through its simplified route, such as laundry detergents and soaps. Disinfectants are not on that list, so expect a fuller registration process for any product sold as a disinfectant, and speak to your NAFDAC state office before you sell one under that name.

blocks.title: Bleach is a separate product line
blocks.text: If you also repackage household bleach, never mix it with your disinfectant cleaner, toilet gel or any other product, and never make it in the same drum. Store it in opaque, closed HDPE containers away from sunlight and heat, which weaken it, and well away from your acid materials. Bleach must never be mixed with acids or with ammonia.

Explain contact time in plain words on the label and when you train a customer's cleaners: the surface must **stay wet** with the product for the full time stated. Spraying and wiping dry at once does not give the disinfectant time to work. For large areas, cleaners can apply it with a damp cloth or mop that leaves the surface visibly wet, then leave it before wiping or rinsing. A short demonstration with a timer on your phone makes this rule easy to remember.

Finally, keep each disinfectant batch record with the supplier's sheet and the COA for the BKC lot you used. If a hospital, school or hotel buyer asks how you know the strength is right, those three documents are your answer.

takeaways: Clean first, then disinfect; dirt protects germs
Use the in-use level and contact time from your BKC supplier's sheet
BKC is cationic: pair it only with nonionic surfactants
Make no germ-kill percentage claims without testing, and check the NAFDAC route for disinfectants

activity.title: Batch sheet and jar test
steps: Get the technical data sheet for a BKC product from a supplier and note its in-use level and contact time.
Calculate the BKC 50% needed for a 5 kg batch at that level, with 1% AEO-9.
Make a 500 g sample and run the jar test with a few drops of dish liquid.
Write a full label: directions with contact time, warning panel, and no unproven claims.
activity.evidence: Your calculation, a photo of the jar test, and your draft label.

quiz.q: Why does the toilet gel use AEO-9 rather than SLES?
options: SLES slowly breaks down in strongly acidic products
quiz.explain: Nonionic surfactants such as AEO-9 stay stable at low pH; SLES gradually breaks down there.

quiz.q: A customer says she pours bleach in the toilet after using your gel "for extra power". What should you tell her?
options: That is fine if she waits one minute
Stop: acid plus bleach releases chlorine gas; use one product, flush fully, and never mix them
quiz.explain: Mixing an acid toilet cleaner with bleach releases chlorine gas in a small closed room. The products must never be combined.

quiz.q: Zainab's glass cleaner leaves streaks. Which change should she test first?
options: Use distilled water and lower the SLES slightly
quiz.explain: Streaks usually come from too much surfactant or minerals in the water. Ammonia and bleach are not part of this course for safety reasons.

quiz.q: Using a supplier's in-use level of 0.2% active BKC, how much BKC 50% goes into a 10 kg batch?
quiz.explain: 10 kg x 0.2% = 20 g active; 20 / 0.50 = 40 g of 50% concentrate.

quiz.q: In the jar test, Adaeze's disinfectant turns cloudy when dish liquid is added. What does that show?
options: Cationic BKC is binding with anionic surfactants and losing its effect
quiz.explain: BKC and anionic surfactants form a complex, tying up the BKC so it cannot work.

quiz.q: Which label line is acceptable for a BKC disinfectant cleaner that has not been laboratory tested?
options: Safe to use on cuts and wounds
Clean the surface first, apply and leave wet for 10 minutes as directed
quiz.explain: Directions with the contact time are honest. Germ-kill percentages and disease claims need test evidence, and skin or wound use is not appropriate.

quiz.q: Where should isopropyl alcohol be measured and stored?
options: In a closed container, in a ventilated area with no flames, sparks or smoking
In an open bucket so it can breathe
Next to the gas cooker for warmth
quiz.explain: IPA is highly flammable. Keep it closed, cool and away from any ignition source.

modules.title: Quality Release, Packaging, Pricing and Scaling Up
modules.overview: A product is only ready to sell when it has passed tests you can repeat, sits in a container that suits its chemistry, carries a truthful label and is priced from real costs. This module turns your six products into a range you can release with confidence, sell at a profit and produce at a larger scale, alone or as a cooperative.

lessons.title: Batch release testing: a test card for every product
objectives: Set a target and an acceptable range for each test on each product
Run pH, flow, appearance, stability, fill-weight and performance checks
Decide whether a batch is released, reworked or rejected
Keep retained samples and test records that answer complaints

blocks.text: Quality control means that every batch is checked against the same written standard **before** any bottle leaves your room. Big factories use laboratory instruments. A small producer can do most of the important checks with pH strips, a kitchen scale, a funnel, a phone timer and a few clear bottles. What matters is that the tests are the same every time and the results are written down.

blocks.name: checklist
blocks.caption: A batch is released only when every line on its test card is ticked.

blocks.text: The release test card

head: Product
pH target
Flow or look
Performance check
rows: Uniform, no layers, set flow time
Clear, set flow time in seconds
Clean a greasy tile at label dose
Thick, clings to a tilted tile
Scale removed from a test surface
Jar test stays clear; correct BKC weight on record

blocks.text: Set your own exact targets from your first three good batches. For example, if three good dish batches gave flow times of 20, 22 and 21 seconds through your funnel, you might set a target of 18 to 24 seconds. Write the targets on the card and keep the same funnel for every test.
Five checks on every batch

items: **Appearance and smell**: pour into a clear bottle and look in daylight. Check colour against your reference sample, and look for haze, layers, lumps or floating oil.
**pH**: dip a strip or a calibrated pH pen and compare with the target range.
**Flow (viscosity)**: time 100 ml through the same funnel at room temperature.
**Fill weight**: weigh ten filled bottles after taring the scale with an empty bottle and cap.
**Performance**: one quick, repeatable use test from the card, against your reference sample.

blocks.title: Worked example: releasing a dish liquid batch
blocks.context: For example, Funke checks her 25 kg dish batch number DL-07 before delivery. Her card says: pH 6 to 8, flow 18 to 24 seconds, fill weight at least 515 g in every bottle.
steps: Appearance: clear yellow, matches the reference bottle. Pass.
pH strip: 7. Pass.
Flow: 21 seconds. Pass.
Fill weights of ten bottles: 516, 515, 518, 514, 517, 515, 516, 519, 515, 516 g. The average is 516.1 g, but one bottle is 514 g, below the minimum.
She tops up the 514 g bottle to 515 g, then re-checks five more bottles from the line; all are 515 g or more.
Performance: one dose of 5 ml in 2 litres of water washes the same number of greasy plates as the reference. Pass.
blocks.result: Batch DL-07 is released. Her record shows every reading, the one correction and the re-check, and a 280 g retained sample goes on the shelf labelled DL-07.

blocks.title: Release decision
items: Run all five checks
All pass: release
Fixable fault: rework and retest
Safety or major fault: reject
Record and keep sample
blocks.caption: Every batch ends with a written decision, never a guess.

blocks.text: Stability: will it last on a shop shelf?

Before you launch a new formula, fill three bottles. Keep one at room temperature in the dark, one in a warm place such as a sunny window inside a closed room, and one in the coolest place you have. Check each week for a month: colour change, separation, haze, smell change, mould, bulging or a collapsed bottle. A product that separates in the warm bottle will separate in a hot market stall. Change the formula before selling, not after complaints.
Retained samples and complaints

Keep one small bottle from every batch, labelled with the batch number and date, for at least as long as the product's shelf life. When a customer complains, ask for the batch number from her label, take out your retained sample and the batch record, and compare. If your sample is fine, the problem may be storage or use, and you can show her the right directions. If your sample shows the same fault, you know which batch to recall and what went wrong.

blocks.title: Rework only what is safe to rework
blocks.text: Adding more salt, fragrance or water to correct flow or smell is normal rework. Never try to rescue a batch where you are unsure how much caustic soda, acid or BKC went in. Mark it "rejected", do not sell it, and ask your supplier or a chemist how to dispose of it safely.

blocks.title: Calibrate your tools
blocks.text: Check your scale every week with a known weight, such as a sealed 1 kg bag of sugar that you have weighed on a trusted scale. If you use a pH pen, calibrate it with buffer solutions as the maker's instructions describe.

takeaways: Every product needs a written test card with targets taken from good batches
Check appearance, pH, flow, fill weight and performance on every batch
No bottle below the label fill weight, even if the average is fine
Keep a retained sample per batch to answer complaints

activity.title: Write and use your test card
steps: Choose one product and write its test card with target ranges.
Test one batch (or a test batch) against all five checks.
Weigh ten filled bottles and calculate the average and lowest weight.
Write the release decision and label a retained sample.
activity.evidence: Completed test card with all readings, the release decision and a photo of the labelled retained sample.

lessons.title: Containers, caps and labels that suit each chemical
objectives: Choose a container and cap that are compatible with each product
Write a complete label including directions, warnings and batch code
Use hazard pictograms correctly and avoid misleading claims
Prepare for NAFDAC registration of your laundry detergent

blocks.text: Packaging for cleaning products has two jobs that cosmetics packaging does not. It must **resist the chemical inside** for months, and it must **protect people**, especially children, who may mistake a colourful bottle for a drink. Packaging that leaks, swells or looks like juice is a safety problem as well as a business problem.

blocks.name: label
blocks.caption: The label is a safety document as well as your brand.

blocks.text: Matching container to contents

head: Product
Container
Cap
Why
rows: Screw cap, measuring cap if possible
Alkaline products; HDPE is tough and resistant
Near-neutral; clear PET shows off colour
Low hazard; trigger must lock for transport
Light weakens it; keep it separate

blocks.title: Never use drink bottles
blocks.text: Do not fill cleaning products into used water, soft-drink or juice bottles, or bottles shaped and coloured like drinks. People, especially children, have swallowed chemicals from familiar bottles. Use bottles made for household chemicals, and keep a different look for every product so a toilet gel cannot be confused with a dish liquid.
What the label must carry

items: Product name and type, for example "Lemon Dishwashing Liquid".
Net content in ml or litres, matching your fill weight.
Your business name, address and phone number.
Directions for use with dose and contact time where relevant.
Main ingredients in plain words, for example "anionic surfactants, nonionic surfactants, fragrance, preservative".
Warnings and first aid, including "do not mix with other products" on acid, alkaline and disinfectant products.
Batch number and manufacturing date, plus a best-before or expiry date.
Your NAFDAC registration number once you have it, and never before.

blocks.text: Products that are corrosive or irritant should show the matching **GHS hazard pictogram**: a red-bordered diamond with a symbol. The corrosion symbol (liquid eating a hand and a metal bar) fits strong acids and alkalis; the exclamation mark fits irritants. Copy the pictogram, signal word ("Danger" or "Warning") and hazard statements from the safety data sheet of your main hazardous ingredient as a guide, and do not add pictograms that do not apply.

blocks.title: Worked example: one batch-code system for the whole range
blocks.context: For example, Ifeoma in Asaba sells four products and wants one batch-code system her staff can read at a glance.
steps: She gives each product a two-letter code: LD laundry, DL dish liquid, FC floor cleaner, TG toilet gel.
She adds the production date as year, month, day: 5 October 2026 becomes 261005.
She adds the batch number for that day: 01 for the first batch, 02 for the second.
The second dish batch made on 5 October 2026 is therefore DL-261005-02.
She writes the same code on the batch sheet, the test card, the retained sample and every bottle label.
blocks.result: Any bottle that comes back with a complaint leads Ifeoma straight to one batch sheet, one test card and one retained sample within minutes.

blocks.title: Label check before printing
items: Name and net content
Directions with dose
Warnings and first aid
Batch code and dates
Business contact details
No unproven claims
blocks.caption: Run every new label through this list before you pay for printing.

blocks.text: Registration with NAFDAC

NAFDAC regulates detergents in Nigeria. Its MSME page lists laundry detergents among the simple products that micro and small businesses can register through a simplified route. For micro-scale applicants it asks for evidence of registration with the Corporate Affairs Commission (CAC), a vetting sample with labels, and medical fitness certificates for production staff, and it publishes the fee and the expected processing time. Check the current page or your NAFDAC state office before you apply, because requirements and fees change. Disinfectant claims, as you saw in Lesson 3.3, need a fuller route.
A range that looks like one brand

Use the same brand name, logo position and font on every product, and give each product its own clear colour band, for example green for dish liquid, blue for laundry, red for toilet gel. Customers then recognise your range on a crowded shelf, and staff in hotels or schools can tell the products apart quickly, which is itself a safety feature. Put the product type in large words and the brand in smaller ones: a cleaner in a hurry needs to read "TOILET GEL" before she reads your brand name.

Set the best-before date from your own stability checks, not by copying another brand. If your retained samples still pass the test card after a period you have actually observed, you have evidence for that date; extend it only as your records grow.

blocks.title: Print short runs first
blocks.text: Print a small run of labels for your first batches. You will almost certainly change directions or wording after early customer feedback, and a box of 5,000 outdated labels is wasted money.

takeaways: HDPE suits acids, alkalis and disinfectants; never use drink bottles
Acid and disinfectant products sold to homes should have child-resistant caps
Labels need directions, warnings, batch code, dates and contact details
Laundry detergent is on NAFDAC's MSME simple-product list; check current requirements

activity.title: Design one complete label
steps: Choose one of your products and pick its container and cap from the table, writing one line on why.
Draft the full label text using the checklist, including a batch code in your own system.
Copy the right GHS pictogram and hazard wording from the main ingredient's safety data sheet.
Ask one person who has never seen your product to read the directions aloud and follow them; fix anything they misunderstand.
activity.evidence: Your label draft, the container choice note and a note of what the test reader misunderstood and how you fixed it.

lessons.title: Costing a batch, pricing each bottle and choosing sales channels
objectives: Calculate the full cost of a batch, including packaging, labour and overheads
Work out the cost per bottle and set wholesale and retail prices
Compare your price with the market without underselling
Choose the sales channels that fit each product

blocks.text: Many small producers price by copying the bottle next to theirs in the market, then discover months later that they were working for free. The safe method is to cost every batch from your own batch sheet, then check that your price is competitive. Prices of LABSA, SLES and bottles change often in Nigeria, so update your costing sheet every time you restock.

blocks.name: calculator
blocks.alt: A person working with a large calculator
blocks.caption: Cost first, then compare with the market, then set the price.

blocks.text: The four parts of batch cost

items: **Raw materials**: every ingredient, by the weight in your batch sheet, at the price you actually paid.
**Packaging**: bottles, caps, labels and cartons for the number of units the batch fills.
**Labour**: your time and any helper's time, at a fair hourly rate. If you do not pay yourself, you cannot grow.
**Overheads**: a share of rent, electricity, transport, data and phone, PPE and testing materials.

blocks.title: Worked example: costing a 20 kg laundry batch in 1 litre bottles
blocks.context: For example, Chiamaka costs her 20 kg laundry batch from Lesson 2.1. The prices below are illustrative assumptions only, not current market prices; she uses the prices on her own receipts.
steps: Raw materials (assumed prices): LABSA 1.6 kg at about ₦3,000/kg = ₦4,800; caustic soda 0.19 kg at about ₦2,000/kg = ₦380; SLES 1.2 kg at about ₦2,500/kg = ₦3,000; soda ash 0.2 kg at about ₦1,200/kg = ₦240; CMC 0.06 kg at about ₦4,000/kg = ₦240; fragrance 0.06 kg at about ₦15,000/kg = ₦900; colour and preservative ₦600; water ₦200. Total raw materials: ₦10,360.
Units: density 1.02 g/ml, so each 1 litre bottle takes 1,020 g. 20,000 / 1,020 = 19.6, so 19 full bottles, with 620 g kept as a retained sample and for testing.
Packaging: 19 bottles x (₦250 bottle and cap + ₦60 label) = 19 x ₦310 = ₦5,890.
Labour: 4 hours at ₦1,000 per hour = ₦4,000. Overheads share: ₦1,500.
Cost per bottle: 21,750 / 19 = about ₦1,145.
blocks.result: Each 1 litre bottle costs Chiamaka about ₦1,145 to make. Any price below that loses money, even if the bottle sells quickly.

blocks.text: From cost to price

Next, survey the market: note the price and size of three competing products in the shops and markets where you want to sell. Convert each to price per litre so you compare like with like. Then set two prices: a **wholesale price** for laundries, shops and resellers who buy in quantity, and a **retail price** for single bottles. The reseller needs room to make her own profit between the two.

blocks.title: Worked example: checking the margins
blocks.context: For example, Chiamaka sets a wholesale price of ₦1,700 and a retail price of ₦2,000 per litre, after checking that similar local brands sell at a comparable price per litre (her own survey).
steps: Wholesale profit per bottle: 1,700 minus 1,145 = ₦555, which is 555 / 1,145 = about 48% on cost.
Wholesale profit per batch: (19 x 1,700) minus 21,750 = 32,300 minus 21,750 = ₦10,550.
Retail profit per batch: (19 x 2,000) minus 21,750 = 38,000 minus 21,750 = ₦16,250.
A reseller buying at ₦1,700 and selling at ₦2,000 earns ₦300 per bottle.
blocks.result: Chiamaka knows exactly what each channel earns her, and that labour and overheads are already paid inside the cost before profit is counted.

blocks.title: Where each product sells best
items: Laundries, hostels: laundry kegs
Restaurants, bukas: dish, floor
Homes, market stalls: small bottles
Offices, cleaning firms: sprays, refills
blocks.caption: Match pack size and price list to the buyer type, not one price for everyone.

blocks.text: Sales channels that suit cleaning products

items: **Institutional buyers**: laundries, hotels, schools, hostels, churches and mosques, estates and offices. They buy in kegs on a regular schedule. Offer a sample, a demonstration and a written price list.
**Cleaning companies**: they need concentrates and refills that give a low cost per bucket. Your dilution ladder results are your sales tool.
**Retail shops and market stalls**: smaller bottles, eye-catching labels, and a fair wholesale margin for the shop owner.

**WhatsApp Business**: a catalogue with photos, prices and pack sizes, and a broadcast list for restock reminders. Accept payment by bank transfer or POS through providers such as Moniepoint or Opay, and confirm receipt in your banking app before delivery, not from a screenshot.

blocks.text: Institutional buyers often compare cost per use rather than cost per bottle. Turn your label dose into a simple figure: if a 4 litre keg of floor concentrate makes 80 kitchen buckets, divide the keg price by 80 to show the cost per bucket. A slightly higher keg price can still win if your dose is lower than a competitor's.

blocks.title: Watch for fake payment alerts
blocks.text: Screenshots and SMS alerts can be faked. Always confirm that the money has arrived in your own account, in your bank or wallet app, before releasing goods, especially for large first orders.

takeaways: Batch cost = raw materials + packaging + labour + overheads
Divide by the number of full units the batch fills, not the theoretical maximum
Set wholesale and retail prices, leaving resellers a real margin
Match pack size and channel to the buyer: institutions buy kegs, homes buy bottles

activity.title: Cost and price one of your products
steps: Collect your real receipts for the raw materials and packaging of one product.
Fill a costing sheet with the four cost parts and calculate cost per unit.
Survey three competing products and convert each to price per litre.
Set your wholesale and retail prices and calculate profit per batch for each.
activity.evidence: Your completed costing sheet, market survey notes and price list.

lessons.title: Scaling to 100 kg batches and producing as a cooperative
